children: Investors are increasingly seeking protection against a potential downturn in artificial intelligence stocks and infrastructure investments, turning to options, credit derivatives and new financial instruments tied to computing power as concerns grow about the sustainability of the multitrillion-dollar AI boom.
The rush to hedge follows mounting pressure on technology shares and heavily indebted AI infrastructure providers, The Wall Street Journal reported. The Nasdaq Composite
fell 2.9% Friday, completing its worst month since March 2025, while companies including Alphabet and Intel suffered sharp selloffs amid heightened scrutiny of AI spending.

For investors, the growing demand for protection signals concerns about whether AI-related valuations, capital expenditures and borrowing can be sustained by future earnings. Rising hedging costs could also increase financing expenses for data-center developers and other companies dependent on continued investment in AI infrastructure.
Options trading illustrates the shift in sentiment. Put options tied to CoreWeave

, an AI cloud infrastructure provider, reached record volumes in October, according to Cboe Global Markets. Popular contracts expiring in 2028 would benefit from a decline in CoreWeave shares to $35, compared with approximately $55 recently.
Credit markets are flashing similar warnings. The cost of insuring debt issued by Amazon
, Alphabet
, Microsoft
, Meta Platforms
and Oracle
against default climbed to its highest levels since 2021, according to bond data provider Solve. Oracle
experienced particularly pronounced deterioration, with credit-default swap spreads widening by more than one percentage point.

Meanwhile, trading firms are developing derivatives that allow companies to hedge fluctuations in the cost of renting AI computing capacity. Jump Trading recently established a computing-power trading operation that structures contracts designed to protect infrastructure providers against declining rental rates.
The emerging market reflects the financial risks associated with massive investments in Nvidia

processors. Rental prices for Nvidia B300 chips have risen approximately 56% this year to $7.56 an hour, according to Silicon Data. Infrastructure operators could purchase contracts guaranteeing compensation if those rates fall below predetermined levels.

Susquehanna International Group has also received inquiries from data-center operators and privately held cloud providers seeking protection against falling chip rental prices. Such arrangements could potentially make lenders more willing to finance expensive AI infrastructure projects.

The hedging activity underscores a growing distinction between enthusiasm for AI's long-term potential and concerns about the economics of individual companies. Investors are increasingly examining debt burdens, utilization rates and the profitability of computing infrastructure rather than assuming every participant will benefit equally.

Despite the increased demand for downside protection, hedging remains relatively small compared with the enormous capital committed to AI development. The activity doesn't necessarily indicate investors expect a collapse, but suggests that even committed AI bulls are becoming less comfortable leaving their exposure unprotected.

title: Wall Street scrambles for protection as AI investment risks mount
